title: After 12 years, man receives P12.3 million lotto jackpot
summary: A man who spent more than a decade fighting for his P12.39-million lotto jackpot received his prize yesterday, despite his winning ticket having been partially burned by a flat iron.

blocks.text: Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office (PCSO) general manager Mel Robles turned over the P12,391,600 check to Antonio Mendoza, whose ticket won the Lotto 6/42 draw on Oct. 2, 2014, at the agency’s headquarters in Mandaluyong.

MANILA, Philippines — A man who spent more than a decade fighting for his P12.39-million lotto jackpot received his prize yesterday, despite his winning ticket having been partially burned by a flat iron.
The release of the prize followed a final Supreme Court ruling and an authorization from the Commission on Audit.

Mendoza’s ordeal began after his granddaughter crumpled the winning ticket. His daughter tried to straighten it by ironing it with a piece of cloth, but the ticket became blackened, leaving only portions of its details visible.
The damaged ticket retained the first digits of three number combinations, the lotto outlet, draw and purchase dates and part of the purchase time.

Mendoza presented the ticket to the PCSO on Oct. 5, 2014 and submitted an affidavit explaining what happened. The agency, however, informed him that it could not award the prize because the ticket could no longer be validated.
He sued the PCSO after the agency failed to pay him despite a recommendation from the House of Representatives committee on games and amusements that the prize be awarded to him.
In a decision issued in September 2023, the Supreme Court’s Second Division denied the PCSO’s petition challenging lower court rulings in Mendoza’s favor.
The court ruled that Mendoza had sufficiently established that he selected the winning six-number combination, saying the lotto ticket served as proof of the bettor’s chosen numbers.

It also held that the PCSO’s rules were ambiguous on whether possession of a complete physical ticket was an absolute requirement for payment and that secondary evidence could be considered because the original ticket was damaged.
